Corinthian Church
kuh-RIN-thee-uhn CHURCH
proper noun
The church founded by Paul in the Greek city of Corinth, recipient of his two canonical epistles to the Corinthians.

Biblical Definition

The Corinthian church was the congregation Paul founded in the wealthy, immoral, and cosmopolitan Greek city of Corinth, and it stands in Scripture as the great case study of a gifted but carnal church—rich in grace yet riddled with sin, the recipient of his two searching epistles. The church was truly the church of God, sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, enriched in all utterance and knowledge, coming behind in no gift. Yet it was torn by divisions—I am of Paul, I of Apollos—and Paul had to call them carnal, walking as mere men; it tolerated gross immorality, dragged brother against brother before pagan courts, abused the Lord’s Supper, misused spiritual gifts in disorder, and harbored some who denied the resurrection. To this church Paul wrote the soaring chapter on love and the great chapter on the resurrection, correcting its errors and recalling it to order, holiness, and the supremacy of love. And he reminded them what grace had done: such were some of you—fornicators, idolaters, drunkards—but ye are washed, ye are sanctified, ye are justified. The dictionary reads the Corinthian church as the abiding mirror of a gifted, worldly, struggling congregation: a true church marred by carnality, called back by apostolic correction to unity, purity, and love—a warning that gifts are no measure of maturity, and a comfort that grace can sanctify even a Corinth.

Webster 1828 Definition

The gifted but carnal church Paul founded at Corinth, recipient of his two epistles; torn by division and sin yet truly the church of God, called back to holiness, order, and love.

CORINTHIAN CHURCH, the congregation Paul founded at Corinth.

Truly the church of God, sanctified and enriched in every gift (1Co 1:2).

Yet carnal, torn by envying, strife, and divisions (1Co 3:3).

“Such were some of you: but ye are washed… sanctified… justified” (1Co 6:11).

Called back to unity, purity, order, and the supremacy of love.

Key Scripture

1Co 1:2 — "Unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours:"

1Co 3:3 — "For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men?"

1Co 6:11 — "And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."

2Co 13:11 — "Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you."

Modern Corruption

Corinth’s abundance of gifts amid its carnality warns against measuring spiritual maturity by gifting; the church was called back to holiness, order, and love.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to draw, against a common modern error, is that spiritual gifts are no measure of spiritual maturity. Corinth came behind in no gift—tongues, prophecy, knowledge, utterance abounded—and yet Paul called them carnal, babes in Christ, walking as mere men. The age that prizes spectacular gifting, dramatic experience, and crowded auditoriums as the proof of God’s blessing should sit long with Corinth, where every gift flourished and the love was thin, the unity broken, and the immorality tolerated. Gifts adorn a church; they do not sanctify it.

The principle to recover is the call back to holiness, order, and love. To this gifted and carnal church Paul wrote not to flatter its gifts but to correct its sins—to heal its divisions, purge its immorality, order its worship, and crown all with the love without which the greatest gifts are nothing. He recalled them to what grace had made them: washed, sanctified, justified, though such things some of them had been. The Corinthian church stands as both warning and comfort: a warning that gifting is not godliness, and a comfort that the grace which could sanctify a Corinth can sanctify any struggling church that submits to the Word and presses on to love.
